question: A shop marks an item "was €200, now €80". Why does the crossed-out price work even when it was never charged?
options: People assume it is a real discount
It sets the number you judge €80 against
answer: The first figure becomes the reference point, and €80 is then read as a saving rather than as a price. It works on people who doubt the original price was ever real — which is why the practice is regulated rather than merely mocked.
move: The crossed-out number is not information. It is the ruler.
trap: Thinking the effect depends on believing the old price.
reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974
